title: Aitana and the Foggy Night
summary: Aitana thinks her grandpa's lighthouse is the most boring place in the world. Until, one foggy night, the light breaks down and she discovers who is waiting for it out at sea.

scenes.text:
The van stopped at the end of the stony track, and Aitana climbed out with her little suitcase.

In front of her, high on the cliff, stood her grandpa's lighthouse. It was white and very tall, with a red stripe at the top, like a woolly hat.

Down below, far below, the waves were breaking against the rocks.

"Welcome to my home," said Grandpa Nicolás, and he pushed open the door with both hands.

Inside there was a table, two chairs, a teapot and a staircase that went up and up. No television, no neighbours, no park.

"So what do you do here?" asked Aitana, dragging her feet.

"You look after the light," said Grandpa. "It's the quietest job in the world."

Aitana sighed. To her, quiet mostly seemed boring.

After a nice hot soup, Grandpa hung his cap on a nail.

"Come on," he said. "I'll introduce you to the lady of the lighthouse."

They climbed the spiral staircase together. It was made of iron, and every step rang under their feet like a drum: dong, dong, dong.

Aitana counted twenty steps. Forty. Sixty.

"How many are there?" she panted.

"A hundred and twenty," said Grandpa. "I climb them twice every night, rain or calm. That's why I've got these old crab legs."

Aitana let out a laugh. It bounced around the tower and came back down from the top, smaller.

"Did you hear that?" said Grandpa, with a wink. "The lighthouse laughs too."

At the top, the lamp room was made entirely of glass.

In the middle was a lamp the size of a football, surrounded by hundreds of glass pieces cut like diamonds. Outside, all around the tower, whistled the wind.

"First you clean the glass," said Grandpa, taking a cloth out of his pocket. "No rush. One dirty finger and the light goes shy."

Then he turned a bronze handle, and the heart of the lighthouse began to spin.

The light shot out into the air, very long, and swept across the night. One way, then the other. One way, then the other.

"It doesn't stay still," whispered Aitana. "It's like a star that walks."

She rested her forehead on the warm glass. And without noticing, she forgot all about the television.

That night, tucked in up to her nose, Aitana asked:

"Grandpa, who is the light for?"

Grandpa sat on the edge of the bed with a notebook with worn covers.

"For the fishing boats that come home late. For Don Elías's little boat, because his eyes aren't good any more. And for three winters now, for someone else too."

He opened the notebook. There was a wobbly drawing: two big backs and one small one.

They were whales.

"A mother, a father and a baby," said Grandpa. "They come past here when the water turns cold, and this channel is full of hidden rocks. When the light turns, they see it from below, like a glow on the ceiling of the sea, and they follow the right way."

"And what if one day the light isn't there?"

Grandpa closed the notebook slowly.

"That's why I'm always here."

Three nights later, the fog came.

It wasn't just any fog. It was thick, white and silent, and it swallowed the rocks, the track and even the top of the lighthouse. Aitana held out her hand and couldn't see her fingers.

Far away, in the dark, a boat's engine was coughing.

"A double-work night," said Grandpa. And they climbed the hundred and twenty steps.

The light turned bravely, opening tunnels in the fog. One way, then the other. One way, then the other.

And suddenly, the lighthouse gave a crunch.

The light stopped. It stayed pointing at nothing, still as a sleeping eye.

"Grandpa…" said Aitana, in a very small voice.

Grandpa didn't shout. He didn't run. He crouched down beside the machine and said, very calmly:

"Granddaughter, I need your hands."

The two of them knelt down on the wooden floor.

Grandpa lifted a round lid, and there was the heart of the lighthouse: wheels with teeth, a coiled spring and a chain with a weight on the end, like a giant clock.

"Look," he said, and he put the torch in her hand. "This wheel has a broken tooth, and the motor can't turn it any more. But we can."

"Without the machine?"

"With our hands. Like in my great-grandfather's day," he said, and he smiled. "I push. You count. The light has to go round once every ten seconds. No more, no less."

And so began the longest and loveliest night of Aitana's life.

Grandpa put both hands on the big wheel and pushed. Aitana counted out loud, keeping time with her hand on her knee:

"One. Two. Three… Nine. Ten. Now!"

And Grandpa pushed again.

The light began to turn once more. Not by itself: turning because the two of them were turning it.

After a while, Grandpa's arms were shaking. So he taught Aitana the secret for not getting tired:

"You breathe in while you rest. You breathe out while you push."

Aitana climbed onto a wooden crate and put her little hands next to his big ones. She closed her eyes, took a breath, and pushed too.

Close to midnight, the fog began to come apart in wisps, like cotton wool pulled open.

The light reached far, far out, clean and clear. And down below, Don Elías's boat sounded its horn twice. Aitana understood that it meant thank you.

"Look at the water," said Grandpa, still pushing.

Aitana pressed her face to the glass.

Next to the rocks, three dark shapes were moving along in a line. Two big ones, and a little one in the middle. Every time the light passed over them, their wet backs shone for a moment.

"They're there," whispered Aitana. "They were waiting for us."

"They were waiting for you too," said Grandpa. "Now you look after the light as well."

Then came the singing.

At first it was like a long sigh inside the cliff. Then it rose up through the stones, through the iron of the staircase, through Aitana's feet, all the way to her chest.

It was a deep, round sound that went on and on without breaking.

"What's that?" asked Aitana, her eyes enormous.

"It's them," said Grandpa, and his voice went soft. "Whales sing when the way is clear. It's how they say they've arrived safely."

The baby answered with a higher note. And the three of them sang together, one voice on top of another, like bells under the water.

Aitana didn't move. It felt as if the lighthouse, the sea and she were all one thing, breathing very slowly.

By the time the machine was working again, dawn was breaking behind the fog.

Grandpa carried Aitana down in his arms, step by step, and tucked her in by the window, with two blankets and a seashell in her hand.

"I know why you do this now," she said, her voice all sleepy. "It's not a boring job. It's a job that looks after."

Grandpa kissed her forehead.

"Tomorrow I'll teach you how to clean the glass."

The light of the lighthouse passed slowly across the wall. One way, then the other. One way, then the other.

And Aitana fell asleep, counting to ten.
